title: Sessions stored with Drizzle
idea: Storing sessions in Postgres keeps each login as a row with an owner and an expiry, so sessions survive restarts and are shared by every server.

analogy.text: A hotel's front-desk ledger. The receptionist may change shift, but the ledger still lists each guest, their key number and checkout time.
analogy.breaks: Reading a ledger is cheap; every request here costs a database query.

points: A `sessions` row holds the id, the owning `user_id` and `expires_at`.
Login inserts the row. Only the id travels in the cookie.
Each request runs one query joining `sessions` to `users`, skipping expired rows.
Logout deletes the row. A restart deletes nothing, so sessions survive.

hero.title: A session as a row in Postgres

steps.caption: Ada logs in. Her password checks out, so the server creates a session.
The server inserts one row: a random id (shortened here), Ada's user id and an expiry time.
Only the id goes back, in an `httpOnly` cookie. The browser keeps it.
Each later request carries the cookie. One query finds the row and joins Ada's user record.
The server restarts and forgets everything in memory. The `sessions` table is untouched.
The new process receives the same cookie, finds the same row, and knows Ada.
A day later the row is past its `expires_at`. The query returns no row, so the answer is `401`.
A cleanup query deletes expired rows. Without it, the table keeps them forever.

code.title: A sessions table with Drizzle
code.caption: Real Postgres. These three functions replace the `Map` calls from the last page.

walk.text: `users` has email, hash and role. Each `sessions` row has a text id, an owner and an expiry.
`create table` keeps the demo self-contained. A real project would use migrations.
Insert one row under a random id, valid for 24 hours. Only the id goes in the cookie.
One query joins `sessions` to `users`, skips the hash, and drops expired rows.
Logout deletes the row. Expired rows vanish only when `purgeExpired` deletes them.
Ada gets two sessions, one already expired. Predict each lookup and the purge before you press Run.
A fresh pool stands in for a server restart. Then log out and look the session up again.

pitfalls: Filter on `expiresAt` in every lookup; an expired row still exists in the table.
Delete expired rows regularly, or `sessions` only ever grows.
Select only `id`, `email` and `role` in the join; never `passwordHash`.

quiz.why: Row `a` exists but `expiresAt` is not after `now`, so it fails. `b` passes. `c` has no row.

takeaway: The database, not the process, remembers who is logged in.

starters: Why is `sessions.id` a `text` column and not a serial number?
